summary: For 8–9 year-olds (UK DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'): describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the human digestive system and trace food's one-way journey from mouth to anus. The core idea is a processing pipeline in which food is progressively broken down so useful nutrients can be ABSORBED into the body and waste removed. Keep functions simple (mouth breaks up, oesophagus squeezes, stomach churns, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water, rectum/anus remove waste); defer enzymes and villi to later (KS3). The transitional insight is that the small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood (not 'food just passes through') and that the stomach does not do all the work alone. US note: NGSS has no elementary PE naming digestive organs; body systems as interacting subsystems appear later (MS-LS1-3), so treat as UK-led.
misconceptions: Thinking the stomach does all the digesting and absorbing, rather than most nutrient absorption happening in the small intestine.
Believing food 'just passes through' unchanged, missing that it is progressively broken down and that useful nutrients cross into the blood.
Confusing the small and large intestines — or assuming 'small' means less important — rather than small intestine = nutrient absorption, large intestine = water absorption.
Placing the stomach at the belly button, or imagining a single bag where all food sits, instead of a long connected canal.
Thinking the oesophagus works by gravity ('food falls down') rather than by muscular squeezing (peristalsis), which is why you can swallow lying down.

activities.title: Journey of the food: drive the bite along the canal
steps: Starting with a labelled body outline showing the alimentary canal as one continuous tube from mouth to anus, move a single bite of food step by step along the canal.
At the mouth, show teeth chopping the food smaller and saliva softening it; at the oesophagus, make the tube squeeze the food down (peristalsis); at the stomach, churn it into a mush.

At the small intestine, show tiny nutrient particles crossing the intestine wall and floating into red blood vessels — state in your own words that 'absorb' means the useful bits leave the tube and enter the body.
At the large intestine, show water being soaked up and the leftover waste becoming more solid before it exits at the rectum and anus.
Say aloud the one simple job of each organ as you pass through it.
activities.insight: Digestion is a one-way sequence of transformations, and 'absorb' means nutrients leave the gut and enter the blood to feed the whole body — food does not merely pass straight through unchanged.

activities.title: Hands-on breakdown and squeeze model
steps: Mash a cracker or biscuit with a fork to act as 'teeth' breaking food up, then add a little water as 'saliva' to soften it.
Squeeze the mush along a leg of tights (or a flexible tube) to feel how muscles push food along — this is peristalsis, not food 'falling' by gravity.
Discuss why you can still swallow when lying down, since the oesophagus squeezes food along rather than relying on gravity.
Connect this mechanical breakdown to the parallel Y4 'types of teeth' topic, so the mouth and its teeth are understood as the first stage of digestion.
activities.insight: Mechanical breakdown and muscular squeezing (peristalsis) are physical processes you can enact; the oesophagus moves food by muscle, which is why swallowing works lying down.

activities.title: Label and locate the organs on a body outline
steps: On a body outline, draw or label the alimentary canal as a continuous tube from mouth to anus with each organ in place.
Place the stomach in the upper left (not at the belly button) and show the small intestine as a long, coiled tube.
Write a one-line simple job beside each organ (mouth chews/softens; oesophagus squeezes; stomach churns; small intestine absorbs nutrients; large intestine absorbs water; rectum/anus remove waste).
Optionally, use a labelled tappable torso with myth-buster flaps (e.g. 'does the stomach do all the digesting?', 'where are nutrients absorbed?') to check the named functions.
activities.insight: The digestive organs form one long connected canal with correct positions, not a single 'bag' where all food sits.

activities.title: Order the journey and distinguish the two intestines
steps: Put the organs in the order food travels, from mouth to exit.
Match each organ to its simple job.
Answer: where are nutrients absorbed? (small intestine) and where is water absorbed? (large intestine).
Explain why the small intestine's job of absorbing nutrients matters: without it you could eat plenty and still not feed your body.
activities.insight: Confirms the sequence and separates the small intestine (nutrient absorption) from the large intestine (water absorption), surfacing the common conflation and the 'stomach absorbs everything' idea.

checkQuestion: When you swallow a mouthful of food, some people think it just drops into your tummy and sits there until it comes out as waste. Trace where the food really goes after the stomach, and explain what the small intestine does that's so important.
checkAnswer: After the mouth (chewing) and oesophagus, food reaches the stomach (which churns and breaks it down), then passes into the small intestine, where the useful nutrients are ABSORBED into the blood; what's left goes to the large intestine, where water is absorbed and waste is formed before it leaves the body. The small intestine's job — absorbing nutrients — is what lets the food actually feed the body.
